newsitem.title: USA: Californians vote to scrap affirmative action.
newsitem.headline: Californians vote to scrap affirmative action.

text.p: Californians struck a blow at 30 years of U.S. affirmative action policy on Tuesday, voting to scrap many state programmes giving preferential treatment to women and minorities.

California, with its large, ethnically diverse population, is the first state to roll back affirmative action programmes and the referendum was closely watched in other states and the nation's capital.

With almost 80 percent of precincts reporting, Californians voted 55-45 percent in favour of the California Civil Rights Initiative, which bans state and local government affirmative action programmes in public employment, education and contracting in California that are based on race or sex.

"For black people the time has indeed come to let go. We cannot forever look through the rearview mirror at America's mistakes. We must look through the windscreen at its opportunities," Ward Connerly, a black Sacramento businessman who led the campaign for the initiative, said.

The vote came two years after Californians approved another racially charged measure to cut off services to illegal immigrants. That initiative has been tied up in the courts ever since and this latest measure is also expected to face legal challenges.
Affirmative action policies have been used in the United States since the 1960s to expand opportunities for women and racial minorities.
Supporters of the California measure, also known as Proposition 209, said racial and gender preferences were unfair and discriminated against someone else who may be better qualified.
Opponents said minorities and women still faced discrimination in education and the workplace and affirmative action policies were needed to "level the playing field."

Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole and California's Republican Gov. Pete Wilson supported the measure while President Bill Clinton, retired Gen. Colin Powell and civil rights leader Jesse Jackson opposed it.
The bitterly-fought campaign over Proposition 209 twice boiled over into raging controversies.
In September, rock-throwing demonstrators clashed with riot police on a Los Angeles university campus when former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke took part in a debate there on affirmative action.
Supporters of Proposition 209 condemned student leaders for inviting Duke, who was not involved with the initiative, to speak against affirmative action at California State University at Northridge.

Last month, the California Republican Party dropped plans to include a clip of Dr. Martin Luther King's famous "I have a dream" speech in a television commercial in support of Proposition 209 after it caused an uproar.

Several civil rights leaders condemned the use of King's words in the ad and the company that manages the King estate asked the makers of the commercial not to use the slain civil rights leader's words or image.
